author_response_spans.text: ## **GENERAL RESPONSE TO REVIEWER COMMENTS - NCOMMS-24-11301A-Z**

We would like to thank the four reviewers who took the time to provide such detailed, thoughtful, and constructive comments to our manuscript. The consistency between reviewer comments speaks to the care taken in providing this feedback and the need for revisions to our paper.

We note that the majority of comments refer to omissions of study details. Given that this is our first submission to the Nature family of journals, we admit that we have apparently overemphasized brevity. Of course, this error occurred in our attempt to observe the word limits on the main paper and to not overwhelm the reader with too much technical detail. Thankfully, we had already conducted many of the studies necessary to address the reviewers' comments. In most cases, we have decided to include the additional information in the methodology section of the paper or the supplements, as advised by the handling editor, Dr. Sebastian Müller.

The most substantive change to our analysis is the retraining of the ML models to predict CCN concentrations. As correctly pointed out by two reviewers, the previous model showed poor performance for relatively low CCN concentrations (below 300/cm[3] ), yet in those conditions clouds are highly susceptible to aerosol contamination. In response, we retrained the models with a training data set that used triple weighting to the data points in clean conditions (below 100/cm[3] ), which resulted in improved predictive capability in clean conditions without causing a significant loss of predictive capabilities for the overall conditions. In addition, we have added results that showed the good performance of our ML models in moderately clean conditions ( _100/cm[3] <CCN<300/cm[3]_ ). The mean relative errors for the clean conditions are still relatively large, but they provide a useful constraint beyond any currently available remote sensing observations.

Another significant change in our study is the replacement of Merra-2 reanalysis data of T and RH with ERA5 reanalysis data. We compared both reanalysis data sets against the airborne in situ data and found slightly better agreement in RH between ERA5 and the in situ data, likely due to the higher spatial resolution of the ERA5 data by comparison to Merra-2. The use of the ERA5 data as predictors instead of Merra-2 resulted in a modest improvement in predictive performance in most ML models (1-2% lower mean relative uncertainties).

Another important change in our manuscript is the clarification of the purpose of our paper, i.e., to present a paradigm that uses ML algorithms to estimate higher-level aerosol properties using only lidar observables and reanalysis data as predictors. These ML models are based on collocated aircraft data for training and testing. The paradigm can be applied to future satellite (or suborbital) observations after training the models to use the available sets of lidar observables as predictors. This purpose is different from presenting a final set of ML algorithms to predict ABS and CCN. As a matter of fact, we fully expect that future ML models that use lidar observations as input can be further optimized with evolving ML techniques and additional training data.

We investigated several potential issues that were raised by the reviewers regarding the robustness of our ML predictions with respect to the selection of a specific reanalysis data set, the collocation criteria and potential spatial auto-correlation of our training data, details of the lidar and in situ measurements that constitute our training data set, and the transferability of our ML models that are trained with four limited-area field campaigns to global data.

Below, we have enumerated our responses, to make it easier to refer to responses raised by other reviewers. Our responses appear in italic font and text that was revised in the main manuscript - appears in blue font. Page and line numbers refer to the revised manuscript when viewed in track “ ” changes mode and All Markup visible.

We hope that we have addressed the reviewers' concerns to their satisfaction and that the paper is now acceptable for publication in Nature Communications. Allow us to express our gratitude to the reviewers one more time - we believe that addressing their comments significantly improved the clarity of our manuscript and the merit of our study.

Because the explanatory text in the results section now appears before the text that appeared on page 4, line 14-18 of the original manuscript, we have added the following transition passage on page 5, line 11, in the revised manuscript to address the reviewer’s concern:_

_“In the following section (Results), we provide two separate analyses. The first analysis describes the performance of ML models that use the full set of HSRL-2 observations for training and as input to the ML predictions (section 2.1). The results in section 2.2 describe the potential performance of ML algorithms trained with the lidar observables available for the EarthCARE lidar system ATLID (i.e., aerosol backscatter, depolarization, and extinction at only one wavelength, 355 nm), with a scheduled launch date of May 2024. For this configuration, we provide the predictions of CCN and ABS using the airborne HSRL-2 UV observations as input after applying random uncertainties to the extinction and backscatter data as described in section 2. This exercise is meant to simulate the probable decrease in predictive capabilities of our ML models when they are applied to satellite observations which will necessarily possess larger uncertainties._

_Both analyses provide insights into the usefulness of the ML retrieved higher-level aerosol properties. The airborne HSRL-2 data can be used with their inherent error characteristics, for example, to study the cloud nucleating properties of aerosols along the lidar curtain. The noiseadded UV data in the second analysis are a proxy for future spaceborne UV-only lidar observations, which are certain to possess larger uncertainties due to lower signal-to-noise ratios for spaceborne lidars in general, because of the range-squared dependence of the lidar signal from the laser transmitter system. Hence, the results shown in 2.1 are best-case-scenario ML prediction_

_assessments and are representative of lidars with the HSRL-2 system’s information content and error characteristics. Adaptation to lidar observables available for a single-channel HSRL or Raman lidar system, i.e., aerosol backscatter and depolarization at two wavelengths, 532 nm and 1064 nm, and aerosol extinction at one wavelength, 532 nm, is straight-forward and will be presented in a separate paper. Such a system may better represent the capabilities of the Raman lidar system that may be contributed to the NASA AOS project by the Italian Space Agency. Conceptually, the approach we outline here can be applied to any set of lidar observations. However, the predictive capabilities of the ML model will depend on the accuracy and precision of the lidar observations, the independence of aerosol backscatter and extinction retrievals, and the availability and accuracy of collocated in situ observations to train the ML model.”_

3) In Fig. 2, the errors become larger (even exceeding 50%) when the in-situ CCN and ABS are low. What are the possible reasons for this? (i.e., out of ML prediction range? Measurement uncertainties?)

_Response #12: This issue was raised by reviewer 4 as well and is important, in particular for CCN, as the largest uncertainty in aerosol indirect effects on climate is associated with clean clouds. The reasons for the larger relative uncertainties in our ML predictions at lower CCN are two-fold: (1) physically, the low CCN may well be invisible; the lidar does not actually see them, but the ML algorithm exploits the relationships between the CCN-size particles with the rest of the aerosol size distributions, which determine the aerosol optical properties. At low overall aerosol concentrations the lidar measurements themselves become relatively more uncertain; (2) there is very limited training data available for the clean conditions below CCN<100/cm[3] . The first reason is a physical limitation, one that all lidar-based retrievals of aerosol microphysics are subject to. The second part can be addressed by retraining the ML model with a training data set that assigns additional weighting to the data in clean conditions and/or additional collocated lidar/CCN measurements to be collected in the future. The second reason we have addressed, in as far as possible, as described below._

_In response to the concerns about our ML models in clean conditions, we have pursued two types of analyses. Because of the relatively large uncertainty of our ML predictions in clean conditions, in our first analysis, we pursued a technique that is commonly used in ML algorithms and entails an extra weighting of data points in data-sparse regions, in this case, the clean conditions. This weighting is similar to the weighting of data by the inverse of their uncertainty in other data fitting applications. Specifically, we explored the retraining of our ML models for CCN/ABS with a training data set that assigned extra weighting to the training data in clean conditions (CCN<100/cm[3] ; ABS<1Mm[-1] ). A risk to such weighting of data in specific data ranges is that it can result in less good_

_fitting of the data outside of the extra-weighted data range. We include here a Figure RC1 (for “Response to Comments” 1) that shows the mean relative uncertainty for the ML CCN/ABS predictions (using HSRL-2 data as input, representing the ML model underlying Figure 2 of our manuscript) and varying the extra weighting to the CCN/ABS training data in the clean condition range (CCN<100/cm[3] ; ABS<1Mm[-1] ) up to an additional weighting of 10. Figure RC1 indicates an asymptotic behavior of the CCN mean relative uncertainty MRE (left panel) at an increased weighting of 3, while there is relatively little impact on the mean relative uncertainty in overall conditions (i.e., all predictions). We attribute the relatively low impact on CCN predictions in overall conditions to the relatively small fraction of data in the clean conditions (less than 10% of overall CCN data)._

_Based on this analysis and the importance of CCN retrievals in clean conditions, we have retrained all ML models for CCN predictions in our paper using a triple weighting of CCN training data in clean conditions (CCN<100/cm[3] )._

_For ABS (right panel of Figure RC1), there is an asymptotic value to the MRE for clean conditions starting at an extra weighting of ~6, but there is also a monotonic increase in MRE with extra weighting for overall conditions. The reason for the greater impact of extra weighting of the ABS training data in clean conditions on the overall ABS prediction performance (by comparison to CCN retrievals) is that a relatively larger fraction of ABS data resides in the clean conditions (more than 60% of overall ABS data). Unlike the CCN predictions, the ABS predictions in clean conditions are climatically less important than the predictions at higher absolute ABS. In combination with the increased penalties (i.e., higher MRE for overall ABS conditions), this made us decide to keep all ABS predictions in our paper with equal weighting of all training data, i.e., without adding extra weight to the clean ABS conditions._

_In the second analysis, we quantify the relative uncertainty for our ML-based CCN predictions at multiple pollution levels from clean to polluted, and we show the impact of the increased (triple) weight assigned to CCN training data in clean conditions relative to the original ML predictions that assigned equal weighting to all training data. _Overall, we note that the point of our paper was not to present the ultimate ML model for CCN and ABS predictions, but to instead present the paradigm of estimating ABS/CCN employing only lidar observations and reanalysis data as predictors, using a ML algorithm trained with collocated lidar measurements and in situ observations with the latter representing the truth regarding higher-level aerosol products._
_To summarize the changes made to our manuscript regarding the clean condition performance of our ML models:_
- _A) We have replaced the parts of the abstract indicated below as follows to clarify the paradigm that we aim to present, page 1, line 9:_

_“_ ~~_We describe a new machine learning (ML) based paradigm for deriving vertically-resolved aerosol properties that will help address this insufficiency in aerosol observations. Our paradigm uses highaccuracy suborbital lidar and in situ measurements to train advanced ML algorithms to predict_~~
~~_higher-level aerosol properties from lidar observations only, with reanalysis data providing additional constraints._~~

_To help address this insufficiency in aerosol observations, we describe a new paradigm for deriving higher-level aerosol properties with machine learning (ML) algorithms that use only lidar observations and reanalysis data as predictors. Our paradigm employs high-accuracy suborbital lidar and collocated in situ measurements to train and test a fully-connected neural network (FCNN) algorithm.”_
## _B) We have added the following text at the end of the first paragraph in the introduction section, page 2, line28:_

These ML algorithms are trained with collocated lidar measurements and in situ observations, the latter representing the truth regarding the higher-level aerosol properties. The paradigm is therefore only possible because of the recent collection of carefully coordinated lidar and in situ aerosol observations. We fully expect that future ML models that use lidar observations as input can be further optimized with evolving ML techniques and additional training data.”_
## _C) We have added the following text to page 21,  line 36 of our manuscript:_

“ _During the review of our manuscript, several reviewers commented on the relatively larger uncertainties in our ML predictions of CCN and ABS in clean conditions (i.e., CCN<100/cm[3] ; ABS<1Mm[-1] ). In response, we pursued a technique that is commonly used in ML algorithms and entails an extra weighting of data points in data-sparse regions, in this case, the clean conditions. Specifically, we explored the retraining of our ML models for CCN/ABS with a training data set that assigned extra weighting to the data in clean conditions (CCN<100/cm[3] ; ABS<1Mm[-1] ). A risk to such weighting of data in specific data ranges is that it can result in less good fitting of the data outside of the extra-weighted data range. We investigated additional weighting of data in clean conditions by up to a factor of 10 and found that the mean relative uncertainty (MRE) in CCN could be reduced significantly with an increased weighting of data in clean conditions by a factor of 3, with relatively little impact on the MRE in overall conditions (i.e., all predictions). The improvement in ML predictions at the low CCN range between equal weighting of all data versus triple weighting of the data in clean conditions is illustrated in Figure S5._

_An analogous analysis for extra weighting of ABS training data in clean conditions (not shown) indicated that extra weighting of ABS training data in clean conditions resulted in significantly increased MRE in ABS predictions for all conditions. The reason for the greater impact of extra weighting of the ABS training data in clean conditions on the overall ABS prediction performance (by comparison to CCN retrievals) is that a relatively larger fraction of ABS data resides in the clean conditions (more than 60% of overall ABS data). Unlike the CCN predictions, the ABS predictions in clean conditions are climatically less important than the predictions at higher absolute ABS. In combination with the increased penalties, i.e., the higher MRE for overall ABS conditions, we decided to use equal weighting of all ABS training data._ ”.

4) Compared to RH and T, atmospheric instability is a more direct indicator of updraft determining CCN activation. It could be helpful to improve prediction accuracy if available.

_Response #13: We appreciate the reviewer’s correct assessment of the importance of atmospheric instability and updraft velocities for CCN activation. Our understanding of reanalysis data is that predictions of vertical profiles of equivalent, potential temperature (as an indicator of atmospheric stability) are highly uncertain. Moreover, our ML models do not attempt to predict CCN for a range of atmospheric supersaturations (SS). Instead, we predict CCN at a SS of 0.4%, because that is the SS level of the majority of in situ CCN data we have to train the ML models._

## General response:

We are grateful for the reviewers’ second round of reviews. We humbly request a reconsideration of the recommendations by reviewers 2 and 4, based on new analysis and associated changes to the manuscript described below.

We would like to thank reviewer 4 for the constructive recommendation encapsulated in their statement “ _... the manuscript should show evidence to support comprehensiveness of input data or the ability of the NN to extrapolate to unseen input spaces (unlikely), or the comments in this paragraph should be toned down._ ” Because it is impossible to show the comprehensiveness of input data as no global data sets for CCN or ABS exist, we opted to demonstrate the NN models’ abilities to extrapolate to unseen input spaces. To do so, we provide an analysis that shows ML models trained with data from the ACTIVATE campaign only and the models’ ability to predict CCN and ABS for never-seen-before lidar input data in the other three airborne campaigns. This analysis, summarized in Figures RC1 to RC5 below, revealed some potential remaining insufficiencies in the combined training data set in our main paper, which may limit the applicability of our ML models to all global conditions. The new findings motivated us to (i) “tone down” further any language regarding the global representativeness of our ML models, and (ii) describe the limitations in the training data set we used. We would like to reiterate that the main point of our paper is to present the paradigm for deriving higher-level aerosol properties from ML models that use only lidar and reanalysis data as input - the ML models presented in our paper are not meant to be final and they will only become better in time with future collections of collocated lidar and _in situ_ data.

In summary, **the new analysis indicates that** _**the full set of training data from all four campaigns is necessary to achieve the low uncertainties in the ML predictions of CCN presented in our paper and that the fundamental paradigm introduced in our paper produces accurate predictions of CCN and ABS to within 33% MRE even when applied to never-seen-before data.**_

The new analyses also revealed that in addition to the range of CCN and ABS values in the total training data set of a given ML model, the range covered in the training data set for a given aerosol species is a key determinant of the ML model’s predictive capabilities. To reflect this new finding, we have added a figure to the supplements that illustrates the potential remaining insufficiencies in our combined 4-campaign training data set, and we have added several cautionary comments to the document that describe the broad range of conditions that permit the application of our ML models, but also the models’ non-finality. You will note the smoother CCN frequency distributions in Figure 1 and the newly added Figures S6, S7 and S8, which better represent the continuous sampling of our CCN dataset.

## Article 

## A machine learning paradigm for necessary observations to reduce uncertainties in aerosol climate forcing 

Received: 23 February 2024 Accepted: 20 September 2024 Check for updates 

Jens Redemann & Lan Gao Uncertainties in estimates of climate cooling by anthropogenic aerosols have not decreased significantly in the last two decades, partly because observational constraints on crucial aerosol properties simulated in Earth System Models are insufficient. To help address this insufficiency in aerosol observations, we describe a paradigm for deriving higher-level aerosol properties with machine learning algorithms that use only lidar observations and reanalysis data as predictors. Our paradigm employs high-accuracy suborbital lidar and collocated in situ measurements to train and test two fully-connected neural network algorithms. We use two lidar data sets as input to our machine learning algorithms. The first data set consists of suborbital lidar observations not previously used in the training of the machine learning algorithms. The second data set consists of simulated UV-only observations to preview the algorithms’ predictive capabilities in anticipation of data from the ATmospheric LIDar system on the EarthCARE satellite, which was launched in May 2024. Here we show that our algorithms predict two crucial aerosol properties, aerosol light absorption and cloud condensation nuclei concentrations with unprecedented accuracy, yielding mean relative errors of 21% and 13%, respectively, when suborbital lidar data are used as predictors. These errors represent significant improvements over conventional aerosol retrievals.

Applied to future satellite missions, the paradigm presented here has great potential for constraining Earth System Models and reducing uncertainties in their estimates of aerosol climate forcing and future global warming. 

Anthropogenically produced atmospheric aerosols are estimated to exert an average cooling of Earth’s climate that offsets between onefifth and one-half of the warming induced by greenhouse gasses[1] . While our understanding of the role of atmospheric aerosols in the Earth system has evolved steadily over the past two decades, uncertainties in aerosol forcing of climate have not decreased commensurately between recent IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) reports[2][,][3] . This is partly due to continuous, new discoveries of previously unknown, complex interactions of aerosols with clouds that drive the aerosol indirect radiative forcing. Arguably the most significant hindrance to the reduction of uncertainties in aerosol forcing 

of climate though is the limitation of observational constraints on crucial aerosol properties simulated in Earth System Models (ESMs), e.g., refs. 1, 4. We note that past satellite observations have yielded essential global-scale insights into the distribution of atmospheric aerosols[5][–][8] . Likewise, suborbital measurements have provided insights into aerosol processes by providing high-accuracy measurements not obtainable from space. However, neither type of measurement has yielded the data to constrain aerosol properties and processes in global-scale ESMs to result in notable reductions in uncertainties of aerosol climate forcing, primarily because observations are often limited in accuracy and spatiotemporal resolution and coverage.

Specifically, the vertical distribution of key aerosol properties, particularly in the remote atmosphere and near those types of clouds that are highly susceptible to aerosol-induced modifications, has proven an elusive measurement challenge for the observational community[9] . In this paper, we describe an ML-based paradigm for observations of crucial aerosol properties, specifically aerosol light absorption (ABS) and cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) concentrations, that can be applied to satellite lidar measurements in the next decade, but also to past suborbital lidar observations. These lidar-based ML predictions yield aerosol data in closer proximity to clouds because the active lidar measurements are not subject to some of the artifacts that afflict passive remote sensing of aerosols in the immediate vicinity of clouds[10] . ABS and CCN are aerosol properties that have not been traditionally derived from lidar measurements – we refer to these aerosol properties as higher-level aerosol properties hereafter. We note that our paper intends to present the paradigm of estimating higher-level aerosol properties with ML algorithms that use only lidar observations and reanalysis data as predictors. These ML algorithms are trained with collocated lidar measurements and in situ observations, the latter representing the truth regarding the higher-level aerosol properties. The paradigm is therefore only possible because of the recent collection of carefully coordinated lidar and in situ aerosol observations.

We fully expect that future ML models that use lidar observations as input can be further optimized with evolving ML techniques and additional training data. 

New satellite mission concepts are being developed to address some of the observational gaps in aerosol properties that determine aerosol climate forcing. They typically include multi-angle polarization-sensitive passive remote sensing of column-integrated aerosol quantities and active remote sensing of the vertical distributions of aerosol backscattering, extinction, and depolarization with lidars, e.g., NASA’s Atmosphere Observing System (AOS)[11] , and ESA/JAXA’s EarthCARE (Earth Cloud, Aerosol and Radiation Explorer)[12] . These aerosol retrievals are typically complemented with observations of crucial cloud properties (e.g., cloud droplet number concentration and effective radius, liquid and ice water path) and meteorological conditions (e.g., updraft velocity) to elucidate aerosol-induced changes in cloud properties and lifetimes (e.g., ref. 13). We note that only the lidar observations provide the vertically resolved aerosol information that is crucial for addressing the most uncertain aerosol climate interactions. Hence, the paradigm developed here is primarily aimed at retrieving essential aerosol properties from spaceborne lidar observations expected to be available in the future, either from the recently launched (EarthCARE) or from the AOS project that is currently in development.

Because EarthCARE and its lidar system ATLID[12] (Atmospheric LIDar) were launched recently (May 2024) and their Level 2 data is expected to be released publicly in the spring of 2025, we include ML predictions that use only UV observables in the training of the ML models and then test the models by using noise-added UV lidar observations as input. The actual error characteristics of the ATLID system will ultimately determine the errors in ML predictions that use ATLID observations as input. Nonetheless, we believe that our analysis provides a meaningful bounding exercise for the expected ML predictions based on ATLID observations. 

Most remote sensing of aerosol properties relies on physics-based retrievals in an optimal estimation framework[14] . Physics-based refersto the fact that these retrievals use forward models that describe the complex interactions of electromagnetic radiation with the aerosol itself, but also the Earth’s surface and the atmosphere[15] . More recently, such retrieval approaches have been applied to joint observations from lidars and polarimeters, with great promise for the increased information content from the combined observations[16] . The grand challenges for physics-based aerosol remote sensing include: (a) some details of the underlying electromagnetic scattering processes in forward models (e.g., scattering of polarized radiation with non-spherical 

aerosol particles and polarized surface reflectance) are unknown; (b) uncertainties in a priori retrieval assumptions propagate more or less directly into the retrieved quantities; and (c) the optimal estimation techniques are computationally expensive.

The paradigm shift presented here involves the training of ML models with lidar data and in situ measurements and then applying the models to an arbitrary lidar dataset for the retrieval of vertically resolved higher-level aerosol properties. The ML models are trained using high-accuracy lidar measurements and collocated in situ observations of key aerosol properties that are not traditionally derived from lidar observations alone. Atmospheric reanalysis data are used to constrain the ML predictions further. Because lidar systems anticipated for space deployment in the future will include only a subset of observations of the airborne lidar system we use in the training of our ML models presented here, our models can be applied directly to future satellite missions after retraining them with the available subset of observables for these missions. We illustrate this paradigm by using airborne lidar observations and collocated in situ measurements from four recent airborne field campaigns to train two sets of ML algorithms to predict aerosol light absorption (ABS) and Cloud Condensation Nuclei (CCN), respectively. These higher-level aerosol quantities are arguably the most important aerosol properties for determining aerosol effects on clouds and climate[1][,][17] . The majority of CCN data (>77%) available to this study was measured at supersaturations in the 0.35-0.4% SS range, hence our choice to focus the ML retrievals on CCN~0.4%SS, although we omit the subscript in the remainder of the manuscript for readability. ABS determines the direct interactions of aerosols with solar radiation and it affects clouds by changing local atmospheric heating rates and atmospheric stability[18] . CCN is the fraction of aerosols capable of forming cloud droplets.

Although a fraction of them are too small to be optically active (e.g., ref. 19), they are the key ingredient for understanding how atmospheric aerosols affect cloud droplet number concentrations, and hence the radiative properties, precipitation, and lifetimes of clouds[20][,][21] . 

Our work builds on research in which we have shown that linear regression models between lidar-derived aerosol extinction or backscattering and CCN are aerosol-type specific and only work for a limited range of relative humidities (RH)[22] . This is caused by the non-linear response of aerosol optical properties to RH increases, while CCN concentrations remain constant. The ML models we developed can predict this exact behavior from the in situ observations. Both ABS and CCN are difficult to constrain with current satellite measurements and physicsbased retrieval approaches. However, global observations of their vertical distribution are urgently needed to constrain physical processes and aerosol climate-forcing estimates in ESMs. In the remainder of this paper, we use the term retrieval as a short-hand term for the predictions of the ML models, despite our awareness of the fundamental differences to the physics-based retrievals discussed above.

This system is the most advanced airborne HSRL system currently in operation, providing independent measurements of aerosol backscattering and depolarization at three wavelengths (355 nm, 532 nm, 1064 nm), and aerosol extinction at 355 and 532 nm.

To train the ML algorithms to predict ABS and CCN, we used HSRL-2 data from four airborne measurement campaigns, collocated with accurate in situ observations of the higher-level aerosol observables to be predicted. The airborne measurement campaigns were conducted in the continental US[25] , over the Southeast Atlantic Ocean[26] , near the Philippines[27] , and off the US Atlantic coast[28] , capturing a wide range of aerosol types and environmental conditions (Fig. 1). The ML model trained with, and applied to, the full set of airborne HSRL-2 observations is able to provide vertically resolved CCN to within 30% uncertainty in 85%of allretrievals, when reanalysis data of T and RH are used as additional predictors.

This constitutes a tremendously useful tool for studying CCN concentrations in the vicinity of clouds from past and future airborne HSRL observations. The model that is trained with UV observations and applied to noise-added observations in order to simulate EarthCARE ATLID observations still yields vertically resolved CCN to within 50% uncertainty in 83% of all retrievals. This capability is far beyond any published physics-based lidar retrievals, including recently published efforts using CALIOP lidar measurements by Choudhury and Tesche[30] , hereafter C&T, which provide a general CCN uncertainty of a factor of 2. We note that the methodology developed in C&T was applied to actual satellite observations, while our study applies the ML models to simplistically simulated satellite observations. We note that the lidar measurements we used for training and input to our ML models provide independent measurements of aerosol extinction and backscatter, as a benefit of the HSRL technique. We note further that the uncertainty comparison above is inadequate in a number of ways. The physics-based retrievals are subject to the full range of parametric, structural, forward model, and measurement uncertainties, while our ML prediction errors primarily capture uncertainty in the suborbital data and the ML algorithms themselves, with the latter affected by the quality and comprehensiveness of the training dataset. We include the comparison to the case-by-case analyses in the literature merely as a reference to the current state of global CCN and ABS retrievals. Future applications of ML models to actual satellite observations and their comparison to suborbital observations will have to provide a more complete uncertainty assessment.

## Reanalysis data used as additional predictors in the ML models 

In addition to using the lidar observables as predictors in our ML algorithms, we explored the use of reanalysis data, in particular temperature (T) and relative humidity (RH), as additional predictors. They were added in the input layer at the same level as the lidar observables and their addition did not change the architecture of our ML algorithms. The reanalysis data, sourced from the ERA5 (ECMWF Reanalysis v5) product[34] , were spatiotemporally interpolated to match the lidar data locations. ERA5 reanalysis data has a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25° in the horizontal, 37 pressure levels in the vertical, and a temporal resolution of 1 h. The product is spatially and temporally interpolated to the exact time and location of the airborne data using linear interpolation.

Figure S6 shows the frequency distribution of RH and T in the reanalysis dataset collocated with our lidar and in situ observations in each campaign, similar to the frequency distributions of CCN and ABS in the inset of Fig. 1. We chose T and RH as additional predictors because they describe the thermodynamic state of the atmosphere in which the lidar observations were collected. RH, in particular, determines the size and refractive index of atmospheric aerosols under ambient conditions and thereby the lidar-observed aerosol optical properties, i.e., extinction and backscattering[35] . We note that the frequency distributions of RH and T between the four airborne campaigns in Fig. S6 showed many similarities and significant overlap in RH frequency distributions in particular. Therefore, it seems unlikely that the Fully Connected Neural Networks (FCNN) that we employ inadvertently distinguish and preferentially select training data from any one of the four flight campaigns. The addition of reanalysis data improves the ML retrieval capabilities significantly, as we show above. 

## Features of the ML architecture 

Our ML algorithms are based on Deep Learning (DL) with FCNN. We trained a feedforward neural network regression model using the 

Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm[36][,][37] . While such ML algorithms have been used extensively in the atmospheric sciences and specifically in Meteorology[38] , their use in retrievals of geophysical variables from remote sensing observations is relatively new (e.g., ref. 39). We explored the use of FCNN and Random Forest algorithms for our application. Both methods demonstrated comparable performance in predicting CCN and ABS. However, the training time for the Random Forest algorithm was nearly twice as long as that for the FCNN.

Consequently, FCNNs were chosen for the final model training in this study. For future applications of this proposed paradigm, it is possible to implement other training algorithms within this framework. 

In our DL architecture, the lidar observables and reanalysis data constitute the predictors, while the in situ measured CCN and ABS constitute the algorithm responses. For each algorithm, we use 70% of the available collocated lidar and in situ observations as the training dataset, 15% as the validation dataset, and 15% as the test dataset. The models’ hyperparameters are tuned iteratively using Bayesian optimization. We use 10-fold cross-validation, which means that we train the ML models on subsets of the training data and validate them with the complementary subsets ten times. The training of neural networks largely depends on the selection of optimal hyperparameters (including the number of layers, number of neurons per hidden layer, activation functions, etc.). Therefore, we have included the optimal sets of these important hyperparameters specific to the models we trained for this study in Table S2. Further details of our data selection, along with a description of the FCNN and its setup can be found in Fig. S1, and Tables S1 and S2 in the supplementary information. 

During the review of our manuscript, several reviewers commented on the relatively larger uncertainties in our ML predictions of CCN and ABS in clean conditions (i.e., CCN < 100/cm[3] ; ABS < 1 Mm[−][1] ). In response, we pursued a technique that is commonly used in ML algorithms and entails an extra weighting of data points in datasparse regions, in this case, the clean conditions.

Specifically, we explored the retraining of our ML models for CCN/ABS with a training dataset that assigned extra weighting to the data in clean conditions (CCN < 100/cm[3] ; ABS < 1 Mm[−][1] ). A risk to such weighting of data in specific data ranges is that it can result in less good fitting of the data outside of the extra-weighted data range. We investigated additional weighting of data in clean conditions by up to a factor of 10 and found that the mean relative uncertainty (MRE) in CCN could be reduced significantly with an increased weighting of data in clean conditions by a factor of 3, with relatively little impact on the MRE in overall conditions (i.e., all predictions). The improvement in ML predictions at the low CCN range between equal weighting of all data versus triple weighting of the data in clean conditions is illustrated in Fig. S5. As a result of this analysis, all ML model predictions of CCN in this study use a triple weighting of training data in the clean CCN conditions. 

An analogous analysis for extra weighting of ABS training data in clean conditions indicated that extra weighting of ABS training data in clean conditions resulted in significantly increased MRE in ABS predictions for all conditions. The reason for the greater impact of the extra weighting of the ABS training data in clean conditions on the overall ABS prediction performance (by comparison to CCN retrievals) is that a relatively larger fraction of ABS data resides in clean conditions (more than 60% of overall ABS data). Unlike the CCN predictions, the ABS predictions in clean conditions are climatically less important than the predictions at higher absolute ABS.

In combination with the increased penalties, i.e., the higher MRE for overall ABS conditions, we decided to use equal weighting of all ABS training data.

For the HSRL backscatter data used as input to the ML models, we assigned random noise by assuming a Gaussian distribution, such that the mean of the noise added equals the mean relative difference between the collocated CALIOP and HSRL data. We then propagated the noise in the backscatter data to the extinction observations using uncertainties in lidar ratios published in the literature[40] . In this manner, we created a UV-only dataset of aerosol backscatter, extinction, and depolarization from airborne HSRL-2 measurements that is noisier than the HSRL-2 airborne observations themselves, in an attempt to simulate the error characteristics of the EarthCARE/ATLID system.

Improving our knowledge about aerosol cooling is crucially important to reduce uncertainties in climate assessment. Large-scale observations of aerosol properties are needed to constrain Earth System Models (ESMs). For examples, aerosol light absorption (ABS) and cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) play key roles in estimating aerosol direct radiation and aerosol-cloud interactions effects, respectively, but large-scale observations of these two crucial properties with good accuracy are still lacking. The manuscript of Redemann et al. addresses this problem by combining machine learning algorithm and satellite/in-situ/reanalysis data to predict ABS and CCN. The predictions are significantly improved over conventional aerosol retrievals, with mean relative errors of 19% for ABS and 13% for CCN. The study is well written and structured. Some details about the methodology and its validation are currently missing or need to be better justified. ## **Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):**

The manuscript addresses the urgent need to improve constraints on observed aerosol properties for understanding aerosol direct and indirect effects on climate, both from the pre-industrial period until now and for future climate projections. Rather than using a traditional physics-based forward model to perform the retrieval of aerosol properties, the manuscript proposes to use a feedforward, fully connected neural network (NN), a novel application in this specific domain. Specifically, the NN uses plane-based lidar observations (supplemented with reanalysis products) to predict CCN concentration and aerosol absorption (ABS). The manuscript argues this machine learning model can be applied to future satellite lidar observations with appropriate adjustments to input data (restricting wavelengths of lidar data used as model inputs and adding random noise).

This work demonstrates the major potential of machine learning and lidar observations to revolutionize retrievals of vertically resolved aerosol properties. However, the results currently presented seem to be a stepping stone toward revolutionary aerosol retrievals rather than a fait accompli. The manuscript at present does not include enough information about data measurement and processing and associated variability/uncertainty to access whether this

1). The machine learning models show substantial biases in their predictions of aerosol properties under clean conditions, which are important for estimating climate impacts (major issue 2). Finally, the manuscript does not convincingly demonstrate that the models trained on plane lidar data are transferable to satellite lidar data with only restrictions in inputs and additional input noise (major issue 3). The combination of the issues makes it difficult to evaluate the manuscript’s claim that they demonstrate machine learning can substantially improve observationally inferred aerosol properties relative to present physics-based retrievals.
Major issue 1: Data processing and its associated uncertainties are not adequately described.

The manuscript does not appear to include information on the instruments and processing performed to produce the predicted aerosol properties of CCN and ABS. The co-location procedure used to combine in-situ aerosol measurements and lidar profiles is also very sparsely described. Why were the distance and time values used chosen? How sensitive are the distributions of CCN and ABS data to these choices? (Independent of the ML predictions, the distribution of in-situ points in Figure 2 vs Figure S2 look non-trivially different.) How are multiple observations satisfying co-location requirements combined? What kind variability is present among multiple observations? The text should at least mention and ideally estimate the magnitude of uncertainty/variability introduced by the co-location and data processing algorithms as well as typical instrument errors and counting uncertainties.
Major issue 2: The models presented show strong biases as a function of aerosol absorption and concentration.

Figures 2 and 4 show clear biases in overestimating both CCN and ABS at low values. These biases are not mentioned in the manuscript text and seem to have limited effect on the metrics used to quantify the performance of the NN models because most data points appear to be clustered at intermediate values of CCN and ABS. (This is difficult to say quantitatively because density of points in Figure 2 and 4 are not given and Figure 1 only includes distributions of occurrence frequency of CCN and ABS in each campaign, not the full dataset.) This bias is particularly concerning because better constraints on aerosol properties in clean conditions are needed to reduce uncertainty in aerosol-cloud indirect effects important for climate (Gryspeerdt et al., 2023, https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-23-4115-2023).
Major issue 3: The manuscript does not convincingly demonstrate the transferability of the presented models based on aircraft observations to satellite observations.

Sensitivity test 2 (Figure S3) suggests (unsurprisingly) that the NN models have no capacity to extrapolate. The manuscript does not address the extrapolations likely to be encountered when applying four limited-area field campaigns to global data. While sensitivity test 3 (Figure S4) demonstrates that the NN models can interpolate between values under conditions seen in the field campaigns, it does not show the transferability of the NN models to different meteorological or aerosol conditions outside what was seen in the field campaigns. Additionally, while manuscript

considers restricting lidar input data and random noise to address differences between airborne and satellite measurements, the manuscript does not address differences in airborne and satellite lidar instrument systematics as well as their observing profiles, resolutions, and coverages.

## Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):

The manuscript addresses the urgent need to improve constraints on observed aerosol properties for understanding aerosol direct and indirect effects on climate, both from the pre-industrial period until now and for future climate projections. Rather than using a traditional physics-based forward model to perform the retrieval of aerosol properties, the manuscript proposes to use a feedforward, fully connected neural network (NN), a novel application in this specific domain. Specifically, the NN uses plane-based lidar observations (supplemented with reanalysis products) to predict CCN concentration and aerosol absorption (ABS). The manuscript argues this machine learning model can be applied to future satellite lidar observations with appropriate adjustments to input data (restricting wavelengths of lidar data used as model inputs and adding random noise).

This work demonstrates the major potential of machine learning and lidar observations to revolutionize retrievals of vertically resolved aerosol properties. However, the results currently presented seem to be a stepping stone toward revolutionary aerosol retrievals rather than a fait accompli. The manuscript at present does not include enough information about data measurement and processing and associated variability/uncertainty to access whether this represents an significant additional source of uncertainty presently unaccounted for (major issue 1). The machine learning models show substantial biases in their predictions of aerosol properties under clean conditions, which are important for estimating climate impacts (major issue 2). Finally, the manuscript does not convincingly demonstrate that the models trained on plane lidar data are transferable to satellite lidar data with only restrictions in inputs and additional input noise (major issue 3). The combination of the issues makes it difficult to evaluate the manuscript’s claim that they demonstrate machine learning can substantially improve observationally inferred aerosol properties relative to present physics-based retrievals.

_Response #31: As a point of clarification, we did not mean to suggest that our machine learning models can be applied to future satellite data as they are and the results are by no means a fait accompli. Instead, we are presenting a paradigm that uses ML algorithms to estimate higher-level aerosol properties using only lidar observables and reanalysis data as predictors. These ML models are based on collocated aircraft data for training and testing, and the paradigm can be applied to future satellite (or suborbital) observations after training the ML models to use the available lidar observables as predictors. This is feasible because the suborbital lidar data we use in our study is a superset of probable future satellite lidar observations. This is a nuance, but an important one because the error in predictions of higher-level aerosol properties from future satellite observations will depend both on the fidelity of the ML models AND the error characteristics of the satellite data._

## **Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):**

The authors provided detailed responses to comments that were easy to understand and fairly comprehensive. Given the information these responses, I cannot recommend this paper for publication at this time, following two specific issues.
## Data Representativeness

The authors claim to have demonstrated how their results are globally representative through histogram distributional comparison with one site in the Central United States. Even so, the histogram shown in Figure R3 does not appear to be representative. The CCN distributions in the presented study are fully different than those at SGP. The ABS distributions appear to be similar at first glance, but this is largely due to the power-law-type distribution. By way of example, the second bin reaches above 50% of the first in the SGP data, but is ~30% in the data used in this study. Overall, it is fundamentally misleading to classify this work as “representative” due to the training data alone.

The authors state that this work uses data from three campaigns, though nearly all of it (96%!) is from the ACTIVATE Campaign. That massive proportion largely makes this paper an analysis of ACTIVATE data, with the A.I. model almost exclusively trained on ACTIVATE observation. As the manuscript is currently written, this paper is framed as an analysis of many different campaigns, but no work was done to actually incorporate the other campaign data (e.g., manage imbalance in training data sources).
